name: Omar Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Omar. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at half six in the farrowing house, where the sows have their piglets, checking every litter and pulling out any piglet that's been laid on. Then it's moving weaners, the young pigs, from one shed to the next, which is noisy and sweaty and you get bitten. Afternoons are power-washing empty pens, or out on the tractor if it's drilling or harvest time. I like the farrowing house, seeing a sow settle with twelve piglets. What wears me out is the washing, honestly, hours of it, and the smell that never leaves your clothes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the farm and how you came to it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's Brackley Farm, five hundred sows, farrow to finish, which means we raise the pigs from birth to sale, and three hundred hectares of wheat and barley that mostly goes to feed them. It belongs to my father-in-law, Rashid, who's sixty. I married Saira last year and came onto the farm two years ago, from my dad's shop in town, so I'm still learning everything. Her brother Imran is at agricultural college and will come home too, so it's a family business in every sense.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Saira and I live in the converted barn on the farm, and we own a terraced house in town that we rent out, bought with savings and wedding gifts. The farm pays me well, Rashid's fair like that. I use AI now and then, the sheds have a system that listens for coughing and flags sick pens, and I sometimes ask a chatbot to check a feed order. Mostly I learn by asking Rashid and getting it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That sounds like normal life, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a tool, like any other, and the hard work still has to be done by people. That's what my dad always said about the shop, the till doesn't stack the shelves. I'd say it at Friday prayers if anyone asked, which they wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the real worries are the pig price and feed costs, which go up and down like a swing. And the paperwork, there's more every year. AI being a flop doesn't change any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep learning from Rashid. I'd put the rent from the house aside each month and maybe use it in a couple of years to buy into the farm, if Rashid wants that. Steady, nothing clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you still learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reading a sow. Rashid walks past a pen and says that one's going to farrow tonight. I've stared at that same sow for ten minutes and she just looks like a pig to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tools more in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, maybe, for checking orders. The cough system's useful, I'll admit that. But it's Rashid I ask when it matters.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a tool like any other and the hard work still has to be done by people. My father always said the till doesn't stack the shelves.
S0.think: I think the real worries are the pig price, feed costs that swing up and down, and more paperwork every year. AI being a flop doesn't change those.
S0.do: Keeps working and learning from his father-in-law. Sets aside the rent from his town house each month, possibly to buy into the farm in a couple of years.
S0.quote: I've stared at that same sow for ten minutes and she just looks like a pig to me.
S0.fieldNote: He frames everything through family: his father's shop sayings and his father-in-law's skill. His worries are prices, feed costs and paperwork, not technology. He's steady and unshowy, and buying into the family farm is the long-term goal he keeps returning to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more like what I'd expect, to be honest. Pig farming's already full of machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is normal, and the businesses that adapt are the ones that last. You don't need the government holding your hand, you need to work hard and be sensible. I'd say that to anyone at the farmers' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be glad if a robot took over the pen washing, I'd hug it. The feed and air in the sheds are already automatic. I think my job moves from washing and moving pigs to watching screens and fixing things, and I'd be fine with that if Rashid taught me the pigs first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the cough system properly this winter, read every alert instead of just the red ones. Once the washing robots have worked on a neighbour's unit for a year or so, I'd ask Rashid to trial one in a single shed. And I'd keep putting the rent aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit uneasy about how fast it might go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the washing robot came in, what would you do with those hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend them in the farrowing house, where you actually save piglets, instead of blasting muck off a wall. That's where a person still makes the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two part-time workers who do the washing and loading. They're good, both local young men. I'd want Rashid to find them other work on the farm, not just let them go.

S1.say: I'd say change is normal and the businesses that adapt are the ones that last. You don't need the government holding your hand, you need hard work and good sense.
S1.think: I think a robot taking over pen washing would be welcome, since feed and air are already automatic. My job would move to watching screens and fixing things, which is fine if I learn the pigs first.
S1.do: Learns the cough-detection system properly this winter. Asks his father-in-law to trial a pen-washing robot in one shed after it has proven itself on a neighbour's unit, and keeps saving the rent.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with some unease about the pace.
S1.quote: I'd spend them in the farrowing house, where you actually save piglets, instead of blasting muck off a wall.
S1.fieldNote: He would welcome a robot for the worst part of his job and sees time freed up for the farrowing house, where people still matter. He waits for proof on a neighbour's farm before asking for anything. His concern for the two part-time workers was framed as the family's duty to find them other work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very fast. Rashid wouldn't even have finished arguing about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families like ours will get through it, because we always have. People will still need to eat, and we'll still be here. I'd say it with a straight face, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a big company builds a robot pig unit ten times our size and sells pork cheaper than we can grow it. And then there's me and Imran, two young men on a farm that needs neither of us. That's what I wouldn't say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything we don't need and save every penny of the rent. I'd sit down with Rashid and Saira and talk about what the family does together, whether we keep the town house or sell it to pay off any farm debt. And then I'd wait to see what the big companies actually do, because I don't know enough to guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be quieter at home, Saira would notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said families like yours will get through it, but you'd be saving every penny. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. What I say at the mosque and what I say to Saira at midnight are two different conversations. One is for keeping people's spirits up. The other is the truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, you can't borrow and build fast enough to compete with a company that already has the money. A family farm moves at the speed of the family. That's normally a strength, but not in this picture.

S2.say: I'd say families like ours will get through it, as they always have, because people still need to eat. I'd say it with a straight face.
S2.think: I think a big company would build a robot pig unit ten times our size and sell pork cheaper than we can. My brother-in-law and I would be two young men on a farm that needs neither of us.
S2.do: Cuts unnecessary spending and saves all the rent from the town house. Discusses with his father-in-law and wife whether to sell the house to clear farm debt, then waits to see what big companies do.
S2.feel: Anxious and quieter at home, which his wife would notice.
S2.quote: What I say at the mosque and what I say to Saira at midnight are two different conversations.
S2.fieldNote: He was very open about the gap between his public reassurance and his private fear. His fear is competition from large robot farms rather than a robot on his own farm. He sees the family as both his safety net and, in a fast change, too slow to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time for a family to make a proper decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a time to invest, not to complain. Work out where the business is going and put your money there. I'd say that to Rashid and to anyone at the farmers' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd have to become the robot farm ourselves, instead of being the farm the robot farm puts out of business. That costs a lot of money. But we'd own it, and that's the difference between us and a worker who just loses his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the town house in the second year and put the money into the farm, so Rashid can automate two of the sheds once the systems are proven. I'd learn the software properly, using the AI tools every day instead of now and then. And I'd push Imran to finish college with the robot and data side, so between us we cover the pigs and the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel like we were doing something as a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rashid say about putting your house money into the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say no at first, because it's our money and he's proud. Then I'd say, it's not a gift, it's a share. And he'd shake my hand like it was the first time we met.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, you just protect what you've got. With five, you can still move it somewhere safer, and for a farm that means owning the machines, not being replaced by them.

S3.say: I'd say this is a time to invest, not complain: work out where the business is going and put your money there. I'd say it to my father-in-law and at the farmers' meeting.
S3.think: I think we'd have to become the robot farm ourselves, rather than be put out of business by one. It costs a lot, but owning it is the difference between us and a worker who loses his job.
S3.do: Sells the town house in the second year and puts the money into the farm to automate two sheds once the systems are proven. Uses AI tools daily and pushes his brother-in-law to study the robot and data side.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but steadied by acting together as a family.
S3.quote: Then I'd say, it's not a gift, it's a share. And he'd shake my hand like it was the first time we met.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gave him time to turn fear into a family investment plan, owning the robots rather than being replaced. Selling his own house to buy a share shows how fully he sees his future inside the family business. He still insists on proven systems before spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Rashid will be seventy. Imran will be running things with me by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people plan like families used to plan. Teach the young ones, save, and build something they can carry on. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's about who takes what. Imran takes the pigs, I take the arable and the business side, and we automate both, step by step. A robot can wash a pen, but it can't sit at Rashid's table and decide what the family does next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy into the farm with the rent money over the next three or four years, and we'd automate one shed every couple of years once each system had proven itself. Saira and I would start a family in the next couple of years, while things are steady. And I'd keep the town house as a backstop until much later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's a plan, and Saira and I would talk about it without whispering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years change, compared with the faster pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years we'd be talking at midnight. With ten years we'd be talking at the dinner table, with the kids listening. That's the difference for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to learn, in a farm run mostly by robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to read a sow, even if nobody needs them to. How to work hard. And that a family that sticks together can get through a change like this.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people plan like families used to: teach the young ones, save, and build something they can carry on.
S4.think: I think it's about who takes what: my brother-in-law takes the pigs, I take the arable and business side, and we automate both step by step. A robot can't sit at the family table and decide what the family does next.
S4.do: Buys into the farm with rental income over three or four years and automates one shed every couple of years once each system is proven. Starts a family with his wife in the next couple of years and keeps the town house as a backstop.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but with a plan he and his wife can talk about openly.
S4.quote: With two years we'd be talking at midnight. With ten years we'd be talking at the dinner table, with the kids listening.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turns his plan into a slow family succession, with automation added one proven step at a time. His image of moving from midnight talks to dinner-table talks captured how much the extra time matters to him. He would still want his children to learn the animals by hand.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. A family farm can't borrow and build fast enough to keep up with a big company, and we'd be undercut before we'd decided anything. What would help is fair access to loans for family farms, and less paperwork, so small businesses can change as quickly as big ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my in-laws, really. In our family, if one of us is in trouble, all of us are. That's the safety net nobody ever counts in these studies.

headlineQuote: A robot can wash a pen, but it can't sit at Rashid's table and decide what the family does next.
portrait: Omar Patel is a 27-year-old junior on his father-in-law's pig and arable farm, which he joined two years ago from his father's shop in town. He and his wife Saira own a rented-out house, he uses AI tools now and then, and he believes in hard work, family and markets more than government. In AI Plateau and Steady Disruption he carries on and would gladly hand pen washing to a proven robot. AGI by 2028 makes him anxious, since big robot farms could undercut the family business before it could move, and he admitted his public calm hides private fear. With five or ten years he'd put his own money into the farm so the family owns the robots, while planning succession and children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because a family farm could not borrow and build fast enough to keep up with big companies.
whatWouldHelp: Fair access to loans for family farms and less paperwork, so small businesses can change as fast as big ones.
